cards.front: Recall a key point about Character Creation and Development
cards.back: Every character has a motivation — what they WANT drives every action and line.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Character Creation and Development
cards.back: Super-objective: the character's overarching goal across the whole play; scene objectives are smaller goals within each scene.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Character Creation and Development
cards.back: Status: the power dynamic between characters — it shifts moment to moment and is shown through body language, position and voice.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Character Creation and Development
cards.back: Character arc: how a character changes from beginning to end — static characters stay the same, dynamic characters transform.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Character Creation and Development
cards.back: Multi-roling: one actor playing multiple parts — requires clear physical and vocal differentiation between roles.

cards.front: What should you know about drama exam tips?
cards.back: When analysing character, use the motivation-objective-action chain: What does the character want? What do they do to get it? What prevents them? How do they change? This systematic approach covers all assessment objectives.

What does Laban effort actions mean?

cards.back: Students often make mistakes here. Wrong: A character's personality is fixed — they are either good or bad throughout the play. Correct: Characters are complex and can change. Their status shifts moment to moment; their understanding grows; their objectives clash with other characters'. The best character analysis tracks development and contradictions, not fixed labels.
Describe the character arc of a character from a play you have studied. How does the playwright use this character to communicate a key theme?

Character analysis tests AO1 (knowledge of character terminology), AO2 (analysing how character communicates meaning), and AO3 (performance choices if asked from a performer's perspective). In the written exam, character questions may ask you to analyse from an audience, performer or director viewpoint — always match your response to the perspective asked.
